passages.happening:
A new character enters: the serpent, “more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made” (verse 1). It speaks to the woman with a question: “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’”

The question twists God's words. God had given every tree but one. The woman answers that they may eat from the trees, but not from the tree in the middle, or they will die (verses 2-3). Then the serpent flatly contradicts God: “You will not surely die” (verse 4). It says God is holding back something good: “your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (verse 5).

The woman looks at the tree. It is good for food, pleasing to the eye, and “desirable for obtaining wisdom” (verse 6). She takes and eats. “She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.” Their eyes are opened, but what they see is that they are naked. They sew fig leaves together to cover themselves (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Hebrew listeners would catch a play on words. At the end of chapter 2 the man and woman were ‘naked’ (arummim). Now the serpent is ‘crafty’ (arum). The two words sound almost the same. The innocent couple meets the shrewd serpent.

Serpents meant many things in the ancient world: wisdom, healing, danger, chaos. In the Epic of Gilgamesh the hero finally finds a plant that would make him young again, and while he bathes, a snake steals it and sheds its skin. The hero weeps for his lost chance. Genesis also tells of a snake and a lost chance at life, but here the loss comes from people choosing to disobey, not from bad luck.

Genesis is careful about the serpent. It is one of the creatures “that the LORD God had made”. It is not a rival god. Genesis itself does not call it Satan or the devil. It does not explain where its evil came from.

Watch the small changes. The woman adds “or touch it” to God's command and leaves out his generous ‘freely’. The serpent never asks her to eat. It only makes her doubt that God is good. And the man is not elsewhere. He is “with her”, and silent.
passages.later:
Later Scripture names the power behind the serpent. An ancient Jewish book, the Wisdom of Solomon, says that death came into the world through the devil's envy, which many read as the earliest link between Genesis 3 and the devil. The New Testament says it openly. Revelation calls the devil “that ancient serpent” (Revelation 12:9, 20:2). Jesus calls the devil “a murderer from the beginning” and “the father of lies” (John 8:44).

Paul uses the scene as a warning to churches: “just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:3).

Jesus himself was tempted, in the wilderness rather than in a garden, and he answered the tempter with God's word: “Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Hebrews says he “was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
passages.hard: Is the woman more to blame than the man? Some readers through history have said so, and have used this chapter to treat women as weaker or more easily led astray. The text does not support that. The man was “with her” (verse 6). God's command had been given to him directly (2:16-17). He listened and ate without a word. When Paul explains how sin entered the world, he names Adam: “sin entered the world through one man” (Romans 5:12). One letter of Paul does say that the woman was deceived and the man was not (1 Timothy 2:14), and Christians read that verse in more than one way. But no reading of Genesis lets anyone blame Eve more than Adam, or blame women for the sin of the world. Both ate. Both hid. Both were judged. Both were clothed by God.
passages.asks: Temptation here begins with a question about God's goodness: is he holding out on you? Ask where you have heard that question in your own life. Then notice how sin works: it promises open eyes and delivers shame. Ask what you have reached for, hoping it would make you wise or free, that left you hiding instead.

passages.happening:
In the cool breeze of the day the man and woman hear “the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden”, and they hide among the trees (verse 8).

God calls to the man: “Where are you?” (verse 9). The man answers that he was afraid because he was naked, so he hid. God asks, “Who told you that you were naked?” and then, “Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?” (verse 11).

Then the blame begins. The man says, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it” (verse 12). He blames her, and in the same breath he blames God, who gave her. God turns to the woman: “What is this you have done?” She answers, “The serpent deceived me,” and she too admits that she ate (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers knew God's presence as something holy. The same verb ‘walking’ is used later for God's presence among Israel: “I will walk among you and be your God” (Leviticus 26:12). In the garden, the God who walked with them has become the God they hide from.

God's questions are striking. He does not need information. A God who made the world knows where the man is. His questions are an invitation to come out and tell the truth. They are the questions of someone seeking a person, not just a judge reading charges.

The answers show what sin has done. Before, the man sang of the woman as “bone of my bones”. Now he calls her “the woman whom You gave me” and pushes the blame on her. The bond between them, and their trust in God, are both broken.
passages.later:
The next chapter repeats the pattern. God asks Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” (Genesis 4:9), and Cain answers with a lie and a shrug. The question ‘where are you?’ runs through the whole Bible as God's search for people who have hidden from him.

Jesus describes his own mission in the same way: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). The God who walked in the garden calling ‘Where are you?’ comes looking again in Jesus.

Paul sets Adam and Christ side by side: “just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).
passages.hard:
How does Adam's sin affect everyone after him? Christians call this the doctrine of original sin, and they confess that all people have sinned and need God's rescue: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). But Christians in the West and in the East have explained it differently.

In the Western churches, following Augustine, many teach that Adam's descendants share not only his broken nature but also his guilt. Augustine read a phrase in Romans 5:12 as ‘in whom all sinned’, following its Latin translation.

The Eastern Orthodox churches speak instead of ‘ancestral sin’. They teach that from Adam we inherit death and a tendency to sin, but not his guilt; each person is guilty for his own sins. They read the same phrase in Romans 5:12 as ‘because all sinned’, as most modern Bibles do.

Even scholars of Greek debate exactly what that phrase means. These notes do not settle the question. Both traditions agree on what matters most here: the damage of the first sin reaches every human life, and no one can undo it alone.
passages.asks: Notice how quickly the blame moves: from me, to her, to God, to the serpent. Ask where you do the same. God's first word to sinners is not a sentence but a question: ‘Where are you?’ Ask what it would mean to stop hiding and answer it honestly.

passages.t: The serpent and the woman's seed
passages.happening:
God speaks first to the serpent, and he does not question it. He curses it: “cursed are you above all livestock and every beast of the field!” It will go on its belly and eat dust (verse 14).

Then comes a promise inside the curse: “And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (verse 15).

Enmity means lasting hostility. There will be war between the serpent and the woman, and between their descendants (‘seed’). And the war has an ending: the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head, while the serpent strikes his heel. A blow to the head is fatal. A bite on the heel hurts, but it is not the end.
passages.hearers:
To ‘eat dust’ was a picture of defeat and humiliation. Enemies who were conquered were said to “lick the dust like a snake” (Micah 7:17). The proud serpent that wanted to raise the couple up to be like God is brought down to the dust.

Notice that only the serpent is cursed here, and later the ground (verse 17). The man and the woman are judged, but God does not curse them.

The word ‘seed’ (Hebrew zera) can mean one child or a whole line of children, just as ‘offspring’ can in English. The word will run through the rest of Genesis. God will promise seed to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob again and again. So the first hearers would hear this promise as the start of a thread: God has not given up on the human race. Out of the woman, through whom the serpent attacked, God will bring the one who defeats it.
passages.later:
Christians have long called this verse the ‘first gospel’, the first announcement of good news in the Bible. In the second century Irenaeus, a bishop in Gaul, read the woman's seed as Christ, born of a woman, who crushes the enemy that had taken humanity captive.

The New Testament does not quote the verse word for word, but it echoes it. Paul says Jesus was “born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4). He tells the church in Rome, “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). Hebrews says Jesus shared our humanity “so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). And John writes, “This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

The picture fits the cross: a wounded heel and a crushed head, victory won through suffering.
passages.hard:
Does this verse speak of Christ? Readers answer in two main ways, and the answers do not have to cancel each other.

The ‘first gospel’ reading, held by Christians since at least the second century, hears in ‘He will crush your head’ a promise of one particular descendant of the woman who will defeat evil: Jesus. Some point out that the Hebrew uses a singular ‘he’.

The plainer reading takes ‘seed’ as all the woman's descendants. On this view the verse first describes humanity's long struggle with evil, a struggle humans will finally win. Others answer that the singular ‘he’ is simply the grammar of the singular word ‘seed’, and does not decide the question.

Many Christians hold the two together: the verse promises a long war between humanity and evil, and the New Testament shows how that war is won by one man, Jesus. These notes do not choose between the readings. What all of them hear is hope: in the same breath as judgment, God promises that evil will not win.
passages.asks: Before God says a word about pain and toil, he promises that evil will be crushed. Ask whether you believe that the worst thing in your life is not the last thing. And ask where you are still at war with the serpent, and whether you are fighting alone or trusting the one who crushed its head.

passages.happening:
To the woman God says: “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth; in pain you will bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you” (verse 16).

To the man he says: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life” (verse 17). The ground will produce “thorns and thistles” (verse 18). He will eat bread by the sweat of his brow until he returns to the ground: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (verse 19).

Each judgment touches the heart of each life. For the woman, bearing children and her closest relationship. For the man, the ground and his daily bread. The blessings of chapter 1, to be fruitful and to rule the earth, now come only with pain.
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world childbirth was dangerous. Many women died giving birth. Rachel dies this way later in Genesis (35:16-19). The first hearers knew these words from life.

The same Hebrew word for painful toil is used for the woman's childbearing and the man's farming. Man and woman share one sorrow, each in their own work.

The words about desire and rule are read in two main ways. Some take ‘desire’ as the woman's longing for her husband, which he will use to dominate her. Others note that the same two words, ‘desire’ and ‘rule’, come again in the next chapter, where God tells Cain that sin “desires you, but you must master it” (4:7). On that reading the verse describes a struggle for control: she will want to control him, and he will dominate her. On either reading the verse shows love twisted into a contest. It is not how God made them in chapter 2.

And dust: the man was formed from the ground, and now he will go back to it.
passages.later:
The Bible does not leave the curse where it is. When Noah is born, his father hopes he will bring comfort from “the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed” (Genesis 5:29). Paul says that creation “was subjected to futility” but waits in hope (Romans 8:20-21). Death is called “The last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26). And the Bible's last chapter says, “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:3).

For husbands, the New Testament turns ‘rule’ upside down: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).
passages.hard:
‘He will rule over you’ must be read carefully. It describes what sin will do to the relationship between men and women. It is part of the curse, not a command. God is not telling husbands to rule over their wives here, any more than he is telling farmers to grow thorns. The rest of the Bible works to undo the curse, not to enforce it.

This verse has been used to excuse the domination and abuse of women: to say that a husband's harsh rule is God's will, and that a wife must accept it. That is a terrible misuse of Scripture. It takes a description of what sin has broken and turns it into a rule to obey. Christians who hold different views on roles in marriage agree on this: no reading of this verse gives anyone the right to harm another person.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

Pain in childbirth is also not a personal punishment. A woman who suffers in childbirth, who loses a baby, or who cannot have children has not been singled out by God. The verse describes a broken world, not a sentence on each sufferer.
passages.asks: Ask where you see the curse in your own life: in work that resists you, in love that turns into a struggle for control. Then ask whether you are fighting the curse or quietly living by it. If you are a husband, ask whether you rule or whether you serve as Christ served.

passages.t: Garments of skin, and the guarded way
passages.happening:
After the judgments, the man names his wife Eve, “because she would be the mother of all the living” (verse 20). The name sounds like the Hebrew word for ‘living’. After a sentence of death, he names her for life.

Then God himself makes clothes for them: “And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them” (verse 21). Their fig leaves are replaced by something better, made by God's own hand.

God says the man has become “like one of Us, knowing good and evil”, and must not now “take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever” (verse 22). The sentence breaks off. So God sends the man out of the garden to work the ground (verse 23). He places cherubim, heavenly guardians, on the east side of Eden, “along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Clothing in the ancient world spoke of honour and care. To strip someone was to shame them; to clothe them was an act of kindness or of honour. The word for these garments, ‘tunics’, is the word used later for Joseph's robe (37:3) and for the tunics of Aaron's sons, the priests (Exodus 28:40). The verb ‘clothed’ is used when Moses clothes the priests (Leviticus 8:13). God covers the people who have shamed themselves.

Cherubim would be familiar to the first hearers from Israel's own worship. Cherubim were woven into the veil of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:31), which kept the way into God's holiest place. The guarded garden looks like a closed sanctuary.

East is the direction of leaving. Cain will settle “east of Eden” (4:16). But notice what is guarded: not destroyed, but kept. The tree of life is still there. The way to it is closed, not erased.
passages.later:
Proverbs uses ‘a tree of life’ as a picture of wisdom, but the tree itself does not return to the story until the Bible's last pages, and there the way is open. “Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates” (Revelation 22:14). The leaves of the tree are “for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:2), and “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:3).

The clothing God gives runs through the Bible too. The New Testament speaks of being clothed with Christ and putting on “the new self” (Colossians 3:10). Paul writes, “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Paul sets the whole story of Adam beside Christ: “For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).
passages.hard:
God said, ‘in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die’ (2:17). They ate, and they did not die that day; Adam lived 930 years (5:5). Was the serpent right? Readers answer in more than one way. Some note that the same Hebrew phrase is used when King Solomon warns a man, “On the day you go out and cross the Kidron Valley, know for sure that you will die” (1 Kings 2:37); the man was executed later, but his death was sure from that day. So here, death became certain the day they ate, and being cut off from the tree of life sealed it. Others add that in the Bible, being sent away from God's presence is itself a kind of death. These readings fit together.

A larger question follows: what death entered the world through sin? Some Christians hold that no animal or human died before the first sin, so that all death came through it. Others hold that human death came through sin, while animals died before humans existed. Others hold that the death meant here is mainly spiritual: being cut off from God, the source of life. These views often follow from the different ways of reading Genesis 1. Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it.

Why the garments of skin? Some readers see in the animal skins a first sacrifice, a picture of a death that covers shame. The text does not say so. What it says plainly is enough: God covers them before he sends them out.
passages.asks: Even in judgment, God names life, clothes his people and keeps the tree of life safe. Ask whether you see God only as the one who sent them out, or also as the one who made their clothes. The way back to the tree of life was guarded, not destroyed. Ask what it means for you that the Bible ends with that way open again.
